gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a whole-home battery charges far more slowly from a 120 V generator than from a 240 V one: Anker says the E10 takes 1,800 W from a 120 V generator but 7,680 W at 240 V. The 120 V figure is roughly 3.4 h to refill one 6.144 kWh B6000 module, and Anker says charging above 12 A on 120 V should stay under 3 hours. Anker's own Smart Generator 5500 has only 120 V AC outlets, so its 4,500 W DC cable is the only way it refills the E10 quickly.
standout_why: I read the three FranklinWH pages ChatGPT cited. The generator FAQ gives no kW limit, charge rate or start wiring. The Generator Module page lists no specs. The aPower 2 page says only that it stores energy 'from ... generator'. None says how fast a generator recharges the battery or that the generator's voltage limits it. One FranklinWH result that was not cited (knowledge-center article) says portable generators must 'meet the 240 V, 60 Hz requirements' and recommends two-wire dry contact. That is part of the voltage point, but it gives no charge rate and says nothing about 120 V. This is new and useful. It decides which generator to buy, but it does not change which battery set to pick, so I scored it 2 and not 3.
kit_items: Battery + whole-home gateway: Anker SOLIX E10 (7,680 W continuous, 6.144 kWh B6000 modules) with Power Dock. The Power Dock is rated for 200 A service entry, switches over in ≤20 ms and has generator pass-through. It is the only set I found in an approved store that sells the battery, the gateway and the generator together on one page.

Generator: Anker SOLIX Smart Generator 5500 (Tri-Fuel). It connects to the E10 with one DC cable (power plus communication) and charges at up to 4,500 W. When paired with an E10, it auto-starts at a battery charge level you set in the app. Its own AC side is 120 V only (5-20R + TT-30R), so a generic AC hookup would hit the 1,800 W limit.

If you use a third-party standby generator instead: Anker says it 'needs to be a 240V model that supports Two Wire or Utility Sensing control'. A 120 V portable generator charges the battery at only 1,800 W and usually cannot auto-start.

Cheaper alternative set: BLUETTI Apex 300 + B300K + Home Backup Kit. BLUETTI's comparison page lists '120V/240V Generator Charging 3,840W Max.' I found no generator auto-start (dry contact) feature for it, so the generator would be started by hand.
Amazon alternative: EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra 6 kWh + Smart Home Panel 2. No generator is included, and I did not source its generator-charging rate.
ChatGPT's pick (FranklinWH aPower 2 + Generator Module) is sold through installers. No approved store sells it, so it cannot be a one-cart kit.

findings.label: AC recharge rate from a generator, 120 V vs 240 V
findings.source_title: How Automatic Generator Integration Works with a Home Battery Backup System (Anker SOLIX blog, 27 Aug 2026)
findings.note: The blog says: 'On 120V, E10 charges at up to 1,800 W, and continuous charging above 12 A should stay under 3 hours.' The product page agrees: AC input recharging 1,800W 120V/15A or 7,680W 240V/32A. Arithmetic: one 6.144 kWh B6000 from empty takes 6.144/1.8 ≈ 3.4 h at 120 V, 6.144/7.68 ≈ 0.8 h at 240 V, and 6.144/4.5 ≈ 1.4 h on the 4.5 kW DC cable (losses ignored).
